sections.heading: The questions behind the solutions
sections.text:
A newly published set of ARC solution write-ups has competitors swapping notes on the machinery behind their agents—and asking what their own rivals did differently.

Domdolus Tolus describes compressing a large model and giving it a Python workspace for puzzle-solving. Grigoriy Zatravkin’s ARC-AGI-3 team reports switching from a faster, reduced model to a fuller one during a run. Yi-Chia Chen says infrastructure improvements bought more useful thinking time than the reinforcement-learning experiments she tried.

The conversations extend the speed-versus-quality debate the Goose reported after the bell: competitors are now publishing the systems and asking one another where those trade-offs worked. These are accounts of their own experiments, not independently reproduced results.

sections.heading: Fast first, careful later
sections.text:
Zatravkin and his coauthors describe an agent that began many games at once with a reduced version of Qwen Flash-Next. Later in the run, it restored the model’s removed experts and continued with fewer simultaneous games. The idea was to use speed while many games were making progress, then give harder remaining games a fuller model.

The team says an earlier attempt at a much more aggressive cut doubled throughput while barely moving the public result. A later submission with its live switch achieved its best public score. Those submissions differed in more than the switch, so the board alone cannot isolate its contribution. The authors also describe rolling back other shortcuts when their agent’s behaviour deteriorated, even where a numerical quality check looked reassuring.

sections.heading: A squeeze with a Python lifeline
sections.text:
In ARC-AGI-2, Domdolus Tolus took a different route: a heavily compressed Flash-Next model paired with a live Python workspace. The team says the agent saw the puzzles as images and could test a proposed transformation against the examples before submitting. It also describes shortening the model’s working memory and packing its cache to support many concurrent tasks.

The write-up gives an unusually candid budget, too: the team estimates roughly US$350 in Claude and Google Colab spending. It says the five contributors paid from their own pockets. In the replies, Chen praised the use of the compressed model and asked about its memory method and speculative decoding. Bushi Liu, whose own team wrote about fitting DeepSeek into the same contest hardware, asked whether image input was the crucial ingredient; his team had not observed the same advantage.

sections.heading: Another team buys more attempts
sections.text:
The ARC-AGI-2 write-up by the Kaggle account mp, which the Goose previously reported, treats the twelve-hour limit as a budget for generating useful tokens. The author describes pruning and compressing Flash-Next, then using reinforcement learning to repair some of the damage, while several independent attempts wrote and checked Python programs.

The write-up reports local tests and a public-board submission separately. That distinction matters: neither the team’s local evaluation nor a public-board score is a final private result. mp says the release’s code and model parts will follow; readers should check the original write-up for their availability.

sections.heading: What should the next contest measure?
sections.text:
Sergei Makarov opened a public discussion about whether ARC-AGI-3 had rewarded inference throughput and whether its successor should change the incentives. CPMP argued that efficient code has long been an advantage in Kaggle. Son Pham called efficiency and quality a trade-off to manage, while noting that some improvements can help both.

Chen agreed that the concern was worth considering. She suggested that a fixed model could put more weight on harness design, while a fixed token budget might encourage models that use their tokens better. But she also cautioned that either restriction could narrow the search and miss a promising approach that does not use a large language model at all.

In a separate 5 November discussion, Richard Csaky proposed fewer public examples, less frequent submissions and prizes tied to releasing solutions. Son Pham welcomed the idea and argued for valuing breakthroughs. Zatravkin said milestone sharing had helped the community improve, but worried that it also reduced the variety of approaches. These are competitors’ proposals and impressions, not announced ARC rules.

There is a useful tension in these accounts: more attempts can help, but an acceleration that damages the model or leaves it unable to use its tools may cost more than it gains. The teams are still asking which trade-offs survive a different test set.

ARC’s official timetable lists the winners announcement for 4 December 2026. Until the private evaluation and eligibility checks are complete, the public places remain provisional. The write-ups have opened the workshop doors; the next question is which ideas hold up when the final results arrive.
